Lessons.Title: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Illustrative Mathematics K–5 First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 7 Lesson 10 inspected: teacher lesson, preparation, all three student PDF pages and original single-page blackline A Garden and a Playground four-card master on the owner computer. The two data cards and two problem cards have SEPARATE information. Do not disclose one student’s card to the other before questions and justifications; this is MLR4 Information Gap, not a printable all-data worksheet or two independent trivia questions.

Learning goals: solve rectangular perimeter and area problems; explain and keep units distinct. Source 3.MD.D.8, 3.OA.C.7, 3.OA.D.8. Sequence: True or False: Divide in Parts warm-up 10 min; Rope Off the Garden 15 min; two-card-set Information Gap 20 min; synthesis 10 min; publisher-gated Cool-down Lin’s Garden Fence 5 min. Original source teacher supports MLR1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time and MLR4 Information Gap plus accessibility representation.

Original warm-up shows FOUR truth judgments: 60÷6=10 TRUE; 72÷6=(60÷6)+(12÷6) TRUE because 12=10+2; 78÷6=(60÷10)+(18÷6) FALSE because left 13 but right 6+3=9; 96÷8=(80÷8)−(16÷8) FALSE because left 12, right 10−2=8. A correct true/false label is not the complete original explanation; discuss decomposition and subtraction mistakes with teacher.

Original Activity 10.1: Andre’s school garden measures 30 feet by 8 feet. Rope encircles the rectangle, so required length is perimeter 30+8+30+8=76 linear feet; product 30×8=240 square feet describes AREA, not rope. Diego’s addition strategy works. Clare’s multiplication ALSO can work when it represents paired equal sides 2×30 + 2×8=76; bare 30×8 would not work. Because the source asks whom to agree with AND why, do not hard-code Clare wrong or claim multiplication is inherently area-only.

Original Activity 10.2 source student task PDF contains only the Information Gap PROCEDURE, pause-for-teacher review, card exchange and role swap. Neither card’s numerical information appears on pupil PDF, so all source work must use the separate blackline master. The original master has four printed cards: Problem Card 1 and Data Card 1, and Problem Card 2 and Data Card 2. First round, the problem-card pupil asks precise questions to the data-card pupil without viewing or reading their partner’s card; the data-card pupil asks “Why do you need to know?”; partners repeat until sufficient data and solve independently. Repeat after switching roles with the second pair of cards.

The first original hidden-card mathematical situation has rectangle area in SQUARE METRES and one linear side plus a longer-than-shorter constraint. Its solution is a perimeter in METRES: find missing side by area divided by known side, then add both pairs of sides. The second reverses this: given perimeter and shorter side, use half-perimeter minus known side for longer dimension; multiply dimensions to find SQUARE-METRE area. Exact numerical contents and teacher keys are stored ONLY in internal authoring evidence, not shown in this first-party pupil narrative before the teacher releases cards.

Warm-up truth explanation, area versus perimeter choice, card exchange and teacher checking must preserve the source cognitive work. A student cannot be certified by typing a number or by being shown both cards at once. If the teacher cannot supply or separate the original blackline cards, the hidden-information source activity must remain TEACHER-REVIEWED and not be automatically marked complete.

Source synthesis explicitly compares linear-length perimeter with square-unit area, despite both relying on rectangular side lengths; record similarities and differences as teacher dialogue. The publisher original Cool-down Lin’s Garden Fence is restricted behind login and was neither read nor copied. First-party independent practice is not claimed to replace the source publisher assessment. Stage D, executable tests, academic review and production publication were not performed.

The original publisher Cool-down was not accessed in this first-party lesson. The Information Gap data and question cards are kept separate; no hidden publisher answers are exposed to the other partner.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangle perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: The distance around a rectangular boundary.
KeyConcepts.Example: 30 ft by 8 ft rope-off requires 76 feet.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangle area
KeyConcepts.Definition: The amount of square-unit surface inside the rectangle.
KeyConcepts.Example: 30 ft ×8 ft yields 240 square feet of surface, not rope length.

KeyConcepts.Title: From area and side to perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use division to recover unknown rectangle side before calculating boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Missing length=area ÷ given length; perimeter twice sum.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use source Data Card 1 only after the learner requests the needed information.

KeyConcepts.Title: From perimeter and side to area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Recover second dimension by half-perimeter difference, then multiply.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Other length=P/2−known side; area=both sides multiplied.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use source Data Card 2 only after teacher releases it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information Gap
KeyConcepts.Definition: Partner holds complementary data that must be requested and justified.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never show both cards or volunteer hidden answers before question cycle.
KeyConcepts.Example: Problem Student: Can you tell me... Data Student: Why do you need to know...?

WorkedExamples.Title: Multiple ways to find garden rope
WorkedExamples.Question: Original source garden 30 ft by 8 ft: use addition or multiplication?
WorkedExamples.Method: Both, if they represent boundary, not area.
Steps: Do not confuse with 30×8=240 square feet.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews both Clare and Diego claims contextually, not a single name.

WorkedExamples.Title: New independent perimeter illustration
WorkedExamples.Question: Another rectangle is 9 m long and 4 m wide. What is its perimeter?
Steps: Trace the whole edge as 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 metres.
WorkedExamples.Check: Independent Edulytics example, NOT one of the original hidden card prompts.

WorkedExamples.Title: New independent area illustration
WorkedExamples.Question: An unrelated rectangle is 6 m by 5 m; how many square metres are inside?
Steps: Express units as square metres, not metres.
The resulting 30 square metres is a region measurement, not a length around the border.
WorkedExamples.Check: Independent first-party example; preserve original card disclosure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat multiplication itself as always wrong for perimeter.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 2×30+2×8 correctly groups equal sides, while 30×8 finds area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Evaluate what the factors represent, not just the operation symbol.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Show both cards to both pupils before they ask questions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Destroys the original MLR4 information-gap challenge.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate problem and data cards; teacher checks request-and-justify interaction.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 240 has square-feet units and covers interior, not boundary.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume area and perimeter use same units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Perimeter is one-dimensional length, area counts 2D square units.

SummaryPoints: Four original division true/false values: TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE.
Original rope garden 30×8 ft needs 76 feet around; both grouping multiplication and direct addition can work.
Info Gap original TWO paired problem/data sets must remain hidden until teacher-controlled information exchange.
Solve missing side from area or from perimeter before calculating the requested quantity; unit distinction is essential.
Publisher original Cool-down gated; tests/CI/Stage D and academic verification not run.
